title: Exploratory attack on AudioSeal
text:
Discussion & Limitations
All attacks were tested on a single audio clip from LibriSpeech. Two black-box attacks (random-noise querying and particle swarm optimisation) and one white-box attack (gradient-based PGD) all evaded detection, but only PGD did so while keeping good audio quality (PESQ 3.71, versus about 1.8 to 1.9 for the black-box attacks).
Reversing PGD to forge the watermark worked even better: detection on unwatermarked audio rose from 1% to 100% with almost no audible change (PESQ 4.48). This was possible because AudioSeal’s detector weights are publicly downloadable, which gives an attacker full white-box access, even though the authors’ own paper warns the weights should be kept private.
These results come from one clip and assume white-box access for PGD, so they show what is possible, not how robust AudioSeal is in general. Developing strong black-box attacks remains the realistic open problem. Note also that PESQ is only a proxy for quality: the query and PSO attacks left audible background noise, so a human listener would likely notice the tampering, which undermines them as practical attacks.

Why do I care about this question?
When I joined INVOKE, I knew very little about how politics worked, and I had the impression that most people my age didn’t care about it. That was humbling. I still however, keep my distance from politics itself, but I don’t think the goal is to immerse yourself in it. It’s to understand it well enough to make decisions that are reasoned, not just emotional. I treat this exploration as factual answers to my questions that I otherwise won’t have known unless I did this.

title: NAFAS
text:
Aim
The target audience was Malaysian parents of children with asthma, in line with SDG 3: Good Health and Well-Being. The app has four parts:

Real-time monitor: current AQI, temperature, humidity and pollutant levels (PM2.5, PM10, O₃) for 40 stations, pulled from the WAQI API, with child-specific guidance.
Learn: a guide to childhood asthma, plus charts comparing yearly state-level AQI with national childhood asthma cases (IHME data, stored in SQLite).
Travel: pick an origin, destination and date, and get a forecast AQI and a 5-day outlook for the destination city. Models were pickled and stored here.
Assess: combines live AQI and PM2.5 with the child’s asthma severity to give an outdoor-activity recommendation.

title: NAFAS
text:
Data and modelling
Historical air quality data was the hardest part. At the time, I couldn’t find a single open source of historical AQI for Malaysia, and the live APIs only returned current readings, so I aggregated daily readings from the api-malaysia repository into a per-city dataset. I then fitted one Prophet time-series model per city (that were available), saved each as a pickle file, and loaded them in the app to forecast AQI for the chosen date.
The forecasts are a proof of concept. Because of time constraints, the models were not rigorously validated, and accuracy drops the further the chosen date is from the training data.
More than anything, this project was my first exposure to how Malaysia could improve on their organization of open-source data.

title: (Demo) Endau: Updating a seat prediction with survey data
text:
The 2026 Johor state election was my first attempt at Bayesian updating, adapted from Rigdon et al. (2009). That paper models a two-party contest. Our version handled several parties at once, using a Dirichlet distribution for each seat’s vote shares.
The model correctly called about 89% of the winning seats (X of Y). I wouldn’t credit the method alone: lucked played a huge part in everything.
The original analysis used my employer’s survey data, which I can’t share. This page is a demo of the core idea on one seat, Endau, using public results from electiondata.my and a synthetic survey.






ImportantThis is a deliberately simple version



The real model had several parties, poststratified by ethnicity, and handled undecided voters. This demo reduces the problem to a two-sided coin: BN (Kak Awi) vs everyone else. It shows the mechanics of Bayesian updating, not how accurate the method is.

title: (Demo) Endau: Updating a seat prediction with survey data
text:
Why Endau
Kak Awi won in 2018 under UMNO and again in 2022 under BERSATU, and she won in 2026 back under UMNO. Endau is a good test of whether a prior built from history can capture a candidate’s personal vote, or only the party’s.

title: (Demo) Endau: Updating a seat prediction with survey data
text:
Limitations
I understood the two-party version of an election model relatively well. Extending it to several parties, in a landscape where coalitions and their members keep changing, was harder, and I can’t say I fully understood every modelling choice. I used AI assistance while building this demo and can explain each step. The main uncertainties in the real model were how party labels map across elections, how much weight history should get, and how undecided respondents are treated.

title: (Demo) Endau: Updating a seat prediction with survey data
text:
Code Demo
Again for context: Kak Awi won in 2018 (UMNO) and 2022 (BERSATU)
Below are the queries that I ran on electiondata.my and later saved for my usage.






NoteQuery used (run on electiondata.my)





SELECT date, election, seat, candidate_uid, name, party, coalition,
       votes, votes_perc, result
FROM headline_ballots
WHERE state = 'Johor'
  AND election IN ('SE-14', 'SE-15')
  AND seat LIKE '%Endau%'
ORDER BY election, votes DESC




Load Data

library(dplyr)
library(readxl)
library(ggplot2)

# import file
res <- read_excel("data/endau-past-results.xlsx") %>%
  mutate(
    # ensuring characters are numbers & date is in correct format
    votes = readr::parse_number(as.character(votes)),
    year  = if (inherits(date, "POSIXct") || inherits(date, "Date")) {
              as.integer(format(date, "%Y"))
            } else {
              as.integer(format(as.Date(date, "%d %b %Y"), "%Y"))
            }
  ) %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  mutate(share = 100 * votes / sum(votes)) %>%
  ungroup()

res %>% select(year, name, votes, share)

# A tibble: 8 × 4
   year name                            votes  share
  <int> <chr>                           <dbl>  <dbl>
1  2018 Alwiyah binti Talib (Kak Awi)    7136 48.0  
2  2018 Norul Haszarul bin Abu Samah     4056 27.3  
3  2018 Roslan bin Nikmat                3689 24.8  
4  2022 Alwiyah binti Talib (Kak Awi)    8433 55.5  
5  2022 Mohd Youzaimi bin Yusof          5392 35.5  
6  2022 Mohammad Fakrulradzi bin Mahmud  1154  7.59 
7  2022 Mohd Noorhisyam bin Ibrahim       145  0.954
8  2022 Ismail bin Don                     77  0.507




Visualization of Endau seat

kak_awi <- res %>%
  filter(grepl("Kak Awi", name)) %>%
  transmute(year, line = "Kak Awi (any party)", share, label = party)

bn <- res %>%
  filter(coalition == "BN") %>%
  transmute(year, line = "BN candidate", share, label = party)

ggplot(bind_rows(kak_awi, bn), aes(year, share, colour = line)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, alpha = .8) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_text(aes(label = label), vjust = -1, size = 3, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(2018, 2022), expand = expansion(mult = c(0.1, 0.25))) +
  labs(y = "Vote share (%)", x = NULL, colour = NULL,
       title = "N.32 Endau: vote share by candidate, not by party")










Constructing Prior
Two priors for 2026, using only the 2018 and 2022 results. Each party’s past share is a blend of the two elections, with the more recent one weighted higher:
\[
p_j = 0.7 \, p_j^{2022} + 0.3 \, p_j^{2018}
\]
The prior is then a Dirichlet distribution, where \(\tau\) is how much we trust history:
\[
\alpha_j = 1 + \tau \, p_j
\]

Party prior: each party keeps its own history.
Candidate prior: Kak Awi’s 2022 share moves with her from PN to BN.


parties <- c("BN", "PN", "PH", "Other")
tau <- 40

# vote share by bucket and year (2018's GS = PAS's bloc, treated as PN lineage)
shares <- res %>%
  mutate(bucket = case_when(coalition %in% c("BN", "PH", "PN") ~ coalition,
                            coalition == "GS" ~ "PN",
                            TRUE ~ "Other")) %>%
  group_by(year, bucket) %>%
  summarise(share = sum(share) / 100, .groups = "drop")

get_share <- function(y) {
  s <- shares[shares$year == y, ]
  out <- s$share[match(parties, s$bucket)]
  out[is.na(out)] <- 0          # party didn't contest that year
  out
}
p22 <- get_share(2022)
p18 <- get_share(2018)

# party prior: each party keeps its history, 70% 2022 + 30% 2018
party_prior <- 0.7 * p22 + 0.3 * p18

# candidate prior: in 2022 only, Kak Awi's share moves from PN to BN
# (2018 needs no swap, she was already UMNO then)
p22_swapped <- p22
p22_swapped[1:2] <- p22[2:1]
cand_prior <- 0.7 * p22_swapped + 0.3 * p18

alpha_party <- 1 + tau * party_prior
alpha_cand  <- 1 + tau * cand_prior

data.frame(parties, p18 = round(p18, 3), p22 = round(p22, 3),
           party_prior = round(party_prior, 3), cand_prior = round(cand_prior, 3))

  parties   p18   p22 party_prior cand_prior
1      BN 0.480 0.355       0.392      0.532
2      PN 0.248 0.555       0.463      0.323
3      PH 0.273 0.076       0.135      0.135
4   Other 0.000 0.015       0.010      0.010




Synthetic Survey
The real survey can’t be shared, so I invented one: 40 decided respondents, drawn from preferences I chose. I set BN near 50% to match the story that Kak Awi’s support followed her to UMNO. That means the demo shows how the update works, not whether the candidate prior is right.

set.seed(42)
n <- 40
true_share <- c(BN = .50, PN = .30, PH = .17, Other = .03)   # invented
survey <- as.numeric(rmultinom(1, n, true_share))
names(survey) <- parties
survey

   24     7     8     1

title: (Demo) Endau: Updating a seat prediction with survey data
text:
Formulation
Let \(p_j\) be party \(j\)’s vote share in the past election, and \(\tau\) how much we trust history. The prior is a Dirichlet distribution with parameters
\[
\alpha_j = 1 + \tau \, p_j
\]
If \(n_j\) survey respondents chose party \(j\), the update is just addition:
\[
\alpha'_j = \alpha_j + n_j
\]
The posterior for the vector of vote shares \(\pi = (\pi_1, \dots, \pi_K)\) is
\[
\pi \mid \text{survey} \;\sim\; \text{Dirichlet}(\alpha'_1, \dots, \alpha'_K)
\]
with mean
\[
\mathbb{E}[\pi_j] = \frac{\alpha'_j}{\sum_k \alpha'_k}
\]
We simulate 10,000 draws from this distribution and estimate each party’s chance of winning as
\[
P(\text{party } j \text{ wins}) = P\left(\pi_j = \max_k \pi_k\right)
\]
which is just the share of draws in which party \(j\) comes first.

title: (Demo) Endau: Updating a seat prediction with survey data
text:
Update: prior + survey = posterior
If \(n_j\) survey respondents chose party \(j\), the update is just addition:
\[
\alpha'_j = \alpha_j + n_j
\]

post_party <- alpha_party + survey
post_cand  <- alpha_cand  + survey


Result

rdir <- function(n, a) {
  g <- matrix(rgamma(n * length(a), a), ncol = length(a), byrow = TRUE)
  g / rowSums(g)
}

summarise_post <- function(a) {
  d <- rdir(10000, a)
  data.frame(party = parties,
             mean = colMeans(d),
             lo90 = apply(d, 2, quantile, .05),
             hi90 = apply(d, 2, quantile, .95),
             win_prob = tabulate(max.col(d), length(a)) / 10000)
}

result <- bind_rows(
  summarise_post(post_party) %>% mutate(prior = "Party prior"),
  summarise_post(post_cand)  %>% mutate(prior = "Candidate prior")
)

result %>% mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3)))

6    PN 0.249 0.174 0.329    0.001 Candidate prior

8 Other 0.029 0.006 0.064    0.000 Candidate prior



plot_df <- bind_rows(
  data.frame(party = parties, share = party_prior, type = "Prior",  prior = "Party prior"),
  data.frame(party = parties, share = cand_prior,  type = "Prior",  prior = "Candidate prior"),
  data.frame(party = parties, share = survey / sum(survey), type = "Survey", prior = "Party prior"),
  data.frame(party = parties, share = survey / sum(survey), type = "Survey", prior = "Candidate prior"),
  result %>% transmute(party, share = mean, type = "Posterior", prior)
) %>%
  mutate(type = factor(type, c("Prior", "Survey", "Posterior")),
         party = factor(party, parties))

  geom_col(position = "dodge", alpha = .85) +
  facet_wrap(~ prior) +
  labs(y = "Vote share", x = NULL, fill = NULL,
       caption = "Survey is synthetic (invented preferences).")










How much does the answer depend on my choices?
Posterior mean for BN, under different trust in history (\(\tau\)) and a survey where her vote did, or did not, follow her:

bn_mean <- function(prior_share, tau, counts) {
  a <- 1 + tau * prior_share + counts
  a[1] / sum(a)
}

set.seed(42)
survey_followed <- as.numeric(rmultinom(1, n, c(.50, .30, .17, .03)))   # BN strong
survey_stayed   <- as.numeric(rmultinom(1, n, c(.35, .45, .17, .03)))   # PN kept the vote

expand.grid(tau = c(10, 40, 100), survey = c("Followed her", "Stayed with PN")) %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(counts = list(if (survey == "Followed her") survey_followed else survey_stayed),
         party_prior = bn_mean(party_prior, tau, counts),
         cand_prior  = bn_mean(cand_prior,  tau, counts)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(-counts) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric) & !tau, ~ round(.x, 3)))

title: (Demo) Endau: Updating a seat prediction with survey data
text:
The idea
This is the globe-tossing example from Statistical Rethinking (ch. 2). Instead of tossing a globe and counting water, I “ask” 40 voters and count BN (Kak Awi). I’m estimating \(p\), BN’s share of the vote, by grid approximation:

Define a grid of possible values of \(p\) (0 to 1)
Define a prior: how plausible each \(p\) looks before the survey, using past results
Compute the likelihood: how well each \(p\) explains “20 of 40 said BN”
Multiply prior by likelihood
Standardise so the result sums to 1. That is the posterior

The starting share blends the two past elections, weighting the recent one more:
\[
p_{\text{history}} = 0.7\,p^{2022} + 0.3\,p^{2018}
\]

In 2018 both lines are the same point, since Kak Awi was the BN candidate. In 2022 they split: she rose to 55% as BERSATU while the BN candidate fell to 35%. This shows her vote held across a party switch. It doesn’t prove the vote followed her, since 2022 was also a national swing towards PN.

title: (Demo) Endau: Updating a seat prediction with survey data
text:
Three starting beliefs, one survey
I compare three priors, so the reader can see how much the answer depends on the starting belief:

Flat: every \(p\) is equally plausible, so the survey decides.
Party: BN keeps its own past share. My belief is centred on that, give or take prior_sd.
Candidate: Kak Awi’s own 2022 share follows her back to UMNO. This is an assumption, and it is the claim being tested.

The survey is synthetic: 20 of 40 decided respondents say BN. I chose this.

# history -> starting shares
bn18  <- res %>% filter(year == 2018, coalition == "BN") %>% pull(share) / 100
bn22  <- res %>% filter(year == 2022, coalition == "BN") %>% pull(share) / 100
awi22 <- res %>% filter(year == 2022, grepl("Kak Awi", name)) %>% pull(share) / 100

p_party <- 0.7 * bn22  + 0.3 * bn18   # BN keeps what the party got
p_cand  <- 0.7 * awi22 + 0.3 * bn18   # Kak Awi's own 2022 share follows her

# synthetic survey
n <- 40; k <- 20

# 1. grid
p_grid <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 200)

# 2. priors ("around this value, give or take prior_sd")
prior_sd    <- 0.1
prior_flat  <- rep(1, 200)
prior_party <- dnorm(p_grid, mean = p_party, sd = prior_sd)
prior_cand  <- dnorm(p_grid, mean = p_cand,  sd = prior_sd)

# 3. likelihood of 20 BN out of 40, at every p
likelihood <- dbinom(k, size = n, prob = p_grid)

# 4 + 5. posterior = prior x likelihood, standardised
update <- function(prior) {
  post <- likelihood * prior
  post / sum(post)
}
post_flat  <- update(prior_flat)
post_party <- update(prior_party)
post_cand  <- update(prior_cand)

c(bn18 = bn18, bn22 = bn22, awi22 = awi22, p_party = p_party, p_cand = p_cand)

     bn18      bn22     awi22   p_party    p_cand 
0.4795377 0.3547135 0.5547661 0.3921608 0.5321976

title: (Demo) Endau: Updating a seat prediction with survey data
text:
What this shows

The same survey gives different answers depending on the starting belief. [Fill in one sentence from your table: which prior ended closest to the survey, and which moved the most.]
How far the belief moves depends on the prior spread (prior_sd) and the number of respondents. Try prior_sd of 0.05 or 0.2, and a different k, and re-run.

title: (Demo) Endau: Updating a seat prediction with survey data
text:
What this doesn’t show

The survey is invented, so this can’t say which prior is right, or how accurate the method is.
Grouping everyone else into one side means “over 50%” is a majority, not “wins the seat”. In a multi-party race BN can win with less.
The 70/30 weights, prior_sd and the candidate prior are judgement calls, not estimates.

}

}








Solid line = posterior, dashed line = prior, grey line = 50%.

Sanity check
With a flat prior, the grid answer should match the exact Beta answer. The difference below should be about zero.

max(abs(post_flat - exact / sum(exact)))

title: Was it worth the flip?
text:
Being very late to the party when it comes to card games, I have since found a fascination towards them. Specifically, a card game called Flip 7, where the goal of the game is to flip 7 distinct cards, without busting.
As simple as it sounds, it’s a probabilistic game. Some would say luck, which it is still, since it’s kinda hard to keep track of how many cards are left. That’s what makes it interesting: the odds change with every card that leaves the deck.

title: Was it worth the flip?
text:
Being very late to the party when it comes to card games, I have since found a fascination towards them. Specifically, a card game called Flip 7, where the goal of the game is to flip 7 distinct cards, without busting.
As simple as it sounds, it’s a probabilistic game. Some would say luck, which it is still, since it’s kinda hard to keep track of how many cards are left. That’s what makes it interesting: the odds change with every card that leaves the deck.

title: Was it worth the flip?
text:
How the game works
Everyone flips cards from a shared deck, one at a time. The deck has number cards from 0 to 12, and there are as many copies of each number as its value (one 1, two 2s, and so on). Flip a number you already hold and you bust, scoring nothing that round. Stop before that happens and you bank the total of your hand. Flip seven different numbers and you earn a bonus, and the first player to 200 points wins. There are also action cards, such as Freeze, Flip Three and Second Chance.

title: Was it worth the flip?
text:
This project
To keep things simple, I only use the number cards 0 to 12 (79 cards) and leave out the bonus cards. The question I want to answer is: when to stop flipping?
Please find the write-up to this here

title: Was it worth the flip?
text:
Code

Create the deck

library(tidyverse)

# create card deck containing 0-5 numbers (for 0 and 1 card, theres 1 each)

deck <- c(0, 1, rep(2,2), rep(3,3), rep(4,4), rep(5,5),
          rep(6,6), rep(7,7), rep(8,8), rep(9,9),
          rep(10,10), rep(11,11), rep(12,12))

[76] 12 12 12 12

# should be 79
length(deck)

[1] 79




Simulate the game

play_round <- function(stop_at){
  
  # randomly shuffle deck
  d <- sample(deck)
  
  # initializing hand and total
  hand <- c()
  total <- 0
  
  for (card in d){
    # the total reaches the limit, then stop
    if (total >= stop_at) return(total)
    
    # if pull the same card, then bust
    if (card %in% hand) return(0)
    hand <- c(hand, card)
    total <- total + card
    
    # whoever gets 7 distinct card gets an additional 15 points
    if (length(hand)==7) return(total +15)
  }
  total
  

  }



Test simulation

# test 
replicate(10, play_round(20))
